title: Classes and objects

youtube.title: C++ Classes and Objects for Beginners | C++ Programming EP 52
youtube.description: In this episode you will define a class with private data and public functions, make objects from a class and explain public and private, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Classes and objects · 1:24 A Counter class · 2:20 Public and private · 2:59 Second program · 4:06 Recap · 4:36 Bug of the Day · 5:29 Challenge · 5:55 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet classes. A class bundles data and the functions that work on it, and it hides the data from the outside.

scenes.onScreen: "Classes and objects": numbered lines (1. A class is a blueprint; 2. An object is one thing built from it; 3. Private data is hidden, public functions are open) and an analogy card: a blueprint and the houses built from it
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A class is a blueprint. An object is one thing built from the blueprint. A class has data and member functions. Data is private by default. Only the class itself can touch it. The public functions are the buttons that everyone may press. Think of a lift. You press a button, but you never touch the motor. A struct and a class are nearly the same in C plus plus. The one difference is the default access. A struct is public by default, and a class is private. By convention, we use a struct for plain data, and a class when the type has rules to protect. A good class hides its data, and it offers a few clear functions.
points: An object is one thing built from it
Private data is hidden, public functions are open

analogy.title: Classes and objects
analogy.body: A blueprint and the houses built from it

scenes.onScreen: counter.cpp: a class with private data and public functions
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] This is the class. [HL 5] The data is private by default. The trailing underscore is a habit that marks member data. [HL 7] Everything below this label is open to all. [HL 8] This function adds one. [HL 9] This function reads the value. [HL 13] Here we make one object. [HL 14] We press the button twice. [HL 16] The count is two. [HL 4] The class is the blueprint. [HL 5] The count is private, so outside code cannot touch it. [HL 7] The word public opens the door for the functions below. [HL 8] Increment adds one to the private count. [HL 9] The word const after the brackets promises that get does not change the object.

scenes.onScreen: a table of what code outside the class may do
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: The table shows the rule. Count is private, so outside code cannot touch it. Increment and get are public, so anyone may call them. This protects the data. Only the class decides how it changes. Notice the line in the picture between the inside and the outside. Outside code may press the buttons, but it cannot reach the data. That wall is what makes classes safe.

diagram.caption: a table of what code outside the class may do

scenes.onScreen: twocounters.cpp: each object has its own data
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 13] We make two objects from one class. [HL 14] Each object has its own count. We add one twice to a. [HL 16] We add one to b once. [HL 17] A has two, and b has one. The objects do not affect each other. [HL 13] Two objects come from one blueprint. Each has its own count. [HL 14] A is increased two times. [HL 16] B is increased one time. [HL 17] The output shows two and one. The objects do not affect each other.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as twocounters dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints two and one. Notice that each object keeps its own state. That is the main idea of objects.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A class is a blueprint, and an object is one thing built from it. Two. Data is private by default. Three. Public member functions are the buttons. Four. Each object has its own data. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A class is a blueprint, and an object is one thing built from it.
Public member functions are the buttons.
Each object has its own data.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Touching private data
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Main tries to set the private count. The compiler says count is private within this context. That is the whole point of private. Use a public function, such as increment, instead. The compiler does not allow outside code to read a private member. This protects the class. If you need the value outside, add a public getter. If you need to change it, add a public function that checks the new value.

scenes.onScreen: I tried to read my class private data. It said, mind your own members.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I tried to read my class private data. It said, mind your own members.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: build a Light class
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a class called Light with a private bool on. Add public functions turn on, turn off, and is on. Hint: keep the bool private, and let three public functions change and read it. Write your answer in the comments.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

counter.cpp: In function 'int main()':
counter.cpp:13:7: error: 'int Counter::count_' is private within this context
   13 |     c.count_ = 5;
      |       ^~~~~~
counter.cpp:5:9: note: declared private here
    5 |     int count_ = 0;
bug.why: Private data is only for the class. Outside code must use the public functions.

pun: "I tried to read my class private data. It said, mind your own members."
challenge: Write a class called Light with a private bool on. Add public functions turn on, turn off, and is on. Hint: keep the bool private, and let three public functions change and read it.
challengeAnswer: Keep the bool private. The functions set it to true or false, and is on returns it. Mark is on as const.
